tldr: In whole-body motion planning for mobile manipulators, this paper freezes a pretrained flow generative model and steers its initial noise (latent space) using reinforcement learning, achieving both higher task success rates and collision avoidance while maintaining fast inference speeds.
hero_caption: Overall framework of RLMM-Flow. It freezes a flow generative policy pretrained on expert trajectories and steers initial latent noise toward better action chunks via offline reinforcement learning.
overview:
Mobile manipulation requires simultaneously coordinating a mobile base and a manipulator arm. It must jointly satisfy numerous constraints, including obstacle avoidance, joint limits, and smooth trajectory generation. Recently, generative policies such as diffusion models and flow matching (generative models that continuously transform simple noise into a data distribution) have gained traction for imitating expert trajectories. However, imitation-only learning cannot push policy performance beyond the distribution of the demonstration data.

To address this, the authors propose "RLMM-Flow," an approach that freezes the weights of a pretrained flow-matching generative model and uses reinforcement learning to steer its input initial latent noise toward more optimal trajectories. Re-training the generative policy itself requires backpropagating through a multi-step ODE generation process, which leads to training instability; steering in the latent space, by contrast, allows stable reward optimization. Furthermore, to stabilize the optimization of high-dimensional trajectory-level latent variables, the framework introduces a warm-up strategy for the action-space critic and a coarse-to-fine latent steering mechanism that progressively expands control from a horizon-shared global trend to step-by-step fine residual adjustments.

Experiments in simulation and on a physical robot (an AgileX Tracer base with a Unitree Z1 arm) demonstrate that this method substantially improves task success rates and drastically reduces collisions compared to imitation-only flow policies and existing RL post-training baselines. In addition, because the generative policy remains frozen, the system eliminates the heavy test-time optimization often required by diffusion models, preserving fast inference speeds.
contributions: Proposed a mobile manipulation framework that unifies whole-body motion generation pretraining via flow matching with offline reinforcement learning post-training in the latent space.
Designed a cascaded latent steering network that predicts base latent variables before arm latents to explicitly capture the dependency between global base movement and local arm manipulation.

Established an action-space critic warm-up strategy and a coarse-to-fine latent steering mechanism that transitions from a coarse trajectory trend to detailed residual corrections, stabilizing high-dimensional latent space optimization.

sections.heading: Beyond the Limits of Imitation: Flow Matching Meets Latent Reinforcement Learning
sections.summary: Mobile manipulators operating in cluttered environments require coordinated whole-body trajectories, but imitation learning alone cannot surpass expert demonstrations. Because applying RL directly to multi-step generative policies is notoriously difficult, this paper proposes steering within the latent space.
sections.details:
To execute tasks in cluttered 3D environments, mobile manipulators must generate base-arm coordinated trajectories in unified action chunks. These chunks must simultaneously satisfy nonholonomic base constraints (such as being unable to slide sideways), manipulator joint limits, collision avoidance, and smoothness. Classical motion planners rely on precise models and require manual per-scene objective tuning. In contrast, modern generative models learn multimodal and temporally consistent motion priors directly from demonstrations. Flow matching, in particular, has emerged as a promising paradigm in robot control because it learns continuous transport from simple Gaussian noise to target trajectories with efficient inference.

However, imitation-only policies cannot exceed the expert distribution, inheriting minor collision risks or inefficiencies present in the dataset. While reinforcement learning (RL) is a natural candidate for refining these trajectories, computing policy gradients or evaluating likelihoods through multi-step Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) is computationally demanding and prone to gradient instability.

One potential alternative is freezing the generative model weights and steering the initial noise space (latent space) using RL. Yet applying this to mobile manipulation faces three major hurdles: (1) latent variables are extremely high-dimensional because they represent an entire trajectory (e.g., 50 steps); (2) the heterogeneous roles of mobile base navigation and end-effector manipulation must be managed jointly; and (3) training a latent critic alongside an action-space critic from scratch creates a moving-target problem, causing learning collapse.

RLMM-Flow overcomes these challenges by introducing cascaded latent steering, an action critic warm-up, and coarse-to-fine latent steering for stable post-training.

sections.heading: At the Crossroads of Generative Policies and RL: Bottlenecks in Prior Work
sections.summary: While trajectory generation using diffusion and flow models has advanced rapidly, post-training them via reinforcement learning remains challenging. Prior latent RL methods assume low-dimensional, homogeneous action spaces, which limits their applicability to high-dimensional 3D whole-body control.
sections.details:
Generative models in robot control have made impressive strides. Diffusion and flow-matching policies enable flexible trajectory generation well beyond unimodal regression models. Combining these models with 3D point cloud encoders like Point Transformer has led to policies (such as 3D Diffusion Policy) that respect geometric spatial structure. In mobile manipulation, frameworks like M2Diffuser generate whole-body trajectories from robot-centric 3D scans, and AC-DiT leverages Transformer architectures. However, these are fundamentally imitation learning approaches and often rely on test-time optimization to enforce physical constraints, incurring a heavy computational cost that severely slows inference.

Meanwhile, efforts to improve generative models using RL rewards—such as Q-filtering, PPO-style fine-tuning, and flow policy gradients—have also progressed. Nevertheless, backpropagating through the entire denoising or transport sequence remains prone to training instability. This motivated approaches like DSRL, which freeze the generator and steer only the initial latent space via RL. Because the frozen generator preserves the pre-learned, smooth trajectory manifold, the output is less likely to produce unnatural or broken motions.

However, existing latent RL methods have primarily targeted single arms or simple simulation tasks with short horizons and homogeneous action spaces. When applied to high-dimensional, point-cloud-conditioned whole-body trajectory planning, they struggle with latent dimensionality explosion and critic instability, failing to work off-the-shelf.

sections.heading: Inside RLMM-Flow: Two-Stage Learning and Three Key Stabilizers
sections.summary: After pretraining a flow policy on high-quality demonstrations, the model is frozen for latent-space reinforcement learning. Key ingredients include a cascaded architecture moving from base to arm, an action critic warm-up, and a coarse-to-fine steering strategy along the time horizon.
sections.details:
RLMM-Flow consists of two stages: pretraining and latent-space reinforcement learning post-training.

### Network Architecture and Input/Output Representations
Following M2Diffuser, the system uses a robot-centric 3D point cloud observation that merges three components: (1) robot points generated via forward kinematics, (2) target points specifying the end-effector goal pose, and (3) scene point clouds representing the environment. Features are extracted using a Point Transformer. An action chunk spans a planning horizon of $H=50$ steps, combining 3-DoF base pose and 6-DoF arm joint angles ($d=9$), resulting in a $50 \times 9$ tensor.

The framework is built around four key networks:
- **Flow Policy**: A Transformer that conditions on point cloud features and time steps to predict the velocity field transporting Gaussian noise into an action chunk.
- **Latent Steering Network $\pi^W$ (Latent Actor)**: Outputs latent vectors in the initial noise space. To reflect the physical dependency where local arm reachability depends on global base positioning, it uses a cascaded Transformer that first predicts base latents, and then predicts arm latents conditioned on them.
- **Action Critic $Q^A$**: Evaluates the quality of generated trajectories in the concrete action space ($50 \times 9$).
- **Latent Critic $Q^W$**: Estimates the value of initial noise vectors to update the latent actor $\pi^W$.

### Stage 1: Flow Model Pretraining
A Rectified Flow policy is trained on an expert dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{IL}}$ containing 9,000 high-quality demonstrations. Instead of uniform time sampling, the authors adopt a Logit-Normal schedule inspired by EDM to sample flow time $t$, focusing training capacity on intermediate noise levels.

### Stage 2: Offline RL in the Latent Space
The pretrained flow policy is completely frozen, and the latent steering actor $\pi^W$ is trained. Several core mechanisms ensure stable optimization:

- **Mixed-Quality Dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{RL}}$**: In addition to 7,500 successful expert trajectories, the dataset includes 1,500 structured suboptimal trajectories (e.g., minor collisions or stopping short of the goal) generated by loosening planner tolerances. This enables the critic to evaluate suboptimal trajectories accurately, preventing value overestimation.
- **$Q^A$ Critic Warm-Up**: In baseline approaches like DSRL-NA, jointly training $Q^A, Q^W,$ and $\pi^W$ from the start destabilizes training because $Q^W$ tries to distill an immature $Q^A$, while $\pi^W$ steers toward an inaccurate $Q^W$. RLMM-Flow addresses this by pausing latent updates ($Q^W, \pi^W$) for the first $N_{\mathrm{pre}}=20,000$ steps, training only $Q^A$ on trajectories generated from standard Gaussian noise.
- **Coarse-to-Fine Latent Steering**: Searching over 50 steps of latent variables from scratch often traps optimization in poor local minima due to high dimensionality. For the actor output $w_{\mathrm{raw}} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times d_w}$, early training ($t < t_{\mathrm{cf}}=50,000$ steps) applies temporal average pooling to create a horizon-shared vector $\bar{w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_w}$, repeating it across all steps as a coarse latent $w_{\mathrm{coarse}}$. This effectively compresses the search space from $50 \times 9$ down to $9$ dimensions to capture global trajectory trends. Only in the later stage is the time-varying residual $w_{\mathrm{res}} = w_{\mathrm{raw}} - w_{\mathrm{coarse}}$ reintroduced with a scaling factor $\lambda_{\mathrm{res}}=0.1$ to refine collision avoidance and terminal accuracy.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Drastic Collision Reductions with Fast Inference
sections.summary: Evaluations across seen/unseen simulation scenes and on a real robot show that RLMM-Flow significantly boosts success rates and collision avoidance over baselines while preserving fast inference speeds.
sections.details:
### Setup and Baselines
Simulations were conducted in indoor environments from PhyScene, evaluating on 900 seen tasks (in-distribution) and 900 unseen tasks (held-out environments). The real-world platform consists of an AgileX Tracer base, a Unitree Z1 arm, and a Livox MID-360 LiDAR, running zero-shot evaluations across 100 trials using point cloud maps built with FAST-LIO2. Tasks are evaluated under strict success criteria (Succ.) requiring goal reach, zero collisions, and joint limit compliance simultaneously, along with collision rate (Coll.), joint violation rate (Joint Viol.), smoothness (Smooth.), and inference runtime (Time).

Baselines include Base Flow (pretraining only), M2Diffuser (diffusion policy with and without test-time optimization), action-space RL baselines (AWR and IQL), and the latent RL baseline DSRL-NA.

### Simulation Results
Key observations from Table 1 include:
- **Pretrained Policy Comparisons**: Base Flow achieved lower collision rates and smoother paths than M2Diffuser without optimization, while executing drastically faster (around 0.15s for Base Flow versus 2.8s for M2Diffuser with test-time optimization).
- **Action-Space RL Baselines**: Direct action-space RL methods like AWR and IQL yielded minimal performance gains over Base Flow and degraded trajectory smoothness. Perturbing entire trajectory chunks directly disrupts the natural coordination learned during pretraining.
- **Latent RL and Component Contributions**: DSRL-NA showed moderate improvements, but critic instability limited its peak performance. In contrast, "RLMM-Flow-QA" (adding only the $Q^A$ warm-up) improved constraint satisfaction, while "RLMM-Flow-CF" (adding only coarse-to-fine steering) significantly lowered collisions. The full RLMM-Flow combining both reached top performance, raising the seen-task success rate from ~61% (Base Flow) to over 80% while sharply cutting collisions. It showed similar strong generalization on unseen scenes.

### Ablation and Training Stability
Reward curves in Figure 6 show that full RLMM-Flow achieves the highest and most stable evaluation rewards. As illustrated in Figure 7, warming up $Q^A$ eliminates steep loss spikes in the latent critic ($Q^W$), providing a stable distillation target.

### Real-Robot Deployment
Deploying policies trained in simulation directly to the physical robot (Table 2) showed the exact same trends. RLMM-Flow maintained high success rates and superior collision avoidance in the real world. Operating without test-time optimization, it easily ran in real time (~0.15s per inference step).

sections.heading: Conclusion: Blending Generative Prior Expressiveness with RL Optimization
sections.summary: RLMM-Flow combines flow-matching pretraining with latent-space reinforcement learning for accurate and safe mobile manipulation. Its simple recipe of critic stabilization and staged latent exploration proves highly effective for high-dimensional control.
sections.details:
This work balances the generative capability of modeling rich motion priors with the optimization strength of reinforcement learning for constrained whole-body mobile manipulation. Freezing the flow model and searching within its initial latent space yields safe, smooth trajectory planning without compromising inference efficiency.

The three design choices—a cascaded base-to-arm structure, action critic warm-up, and coarse-to-fine latent steering—effectively resolve the training instabilities typical of high-dimensional trajectory optimization, offering valuable insights for future research on generative robot policies.

sections.heading: Appendix: Collision Sphere Modeling and Reward Normalization
sections.summary: Approximating the entire robot with link-wise collision spheres enables unified geometric and clearance calculations. In addition, an offline dataset normalization scheme keeps multi-component reward scales balanced.
sections.details:
The appendix details the geometric modeling and reward formulation critical for stabilizing reinforcement learning.

### Whole-Body Modeling via Collision Spheres
The robot's geometry is approximated as a collection of collision spheres placed along the mobile base and arm links. Using forward kinematics (FK), the world-coordinate position of every collision sphere ${}^{W}\mathbf{p}_{l,m}(q_i)$ is computed efficiently at each trajectory step. This unified representation facilitates computing goal attainment (capturing both position and orientation via root-mean-square distance between gripper and target spheres), collision clearance (distance from spheres to environment obstacle points), and trajectory smoothness across time steps.

### Dataset-Level Reward Normalization
The composite reward consists of five raw components: (1) goal reaching $\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{goal}}$, (2) base nonholonomic limit penalty $\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{lim}}$, (3) collision risk penalty $\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{colli}}$, (4) trajectory smoothness penalty $\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{smooth}}$, and (5) arm joint limit penalty $\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{joint}}$.

Because these metrics have completely different physical units and numerical scales, balancing a weighted sum directly is difficult. The authors precompute the mean and standard deviation of each term over the fixed offline dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{RL}}$, apply Z-score normalization, and clip values to $[-5, 5]$. Consequently, reward weights (such as $\alpha_1=1.0$ for goal reaching and $\alpha_3=0.4$ for collision) reflect true task priorities rather than arbitrary scale adjustments, greatly simplifying hyperparameter tuning.

takeaways: When improving multi-step generative policies (Diffusion/Flow) with RL, steering within the initial latent noise space preserves motion naturalness better than directly updating policy weights.
In critic distillation frameworks (Action Critic to Latent Critic), thoroughly warming up the action-space critic first is essential to stabilize the learning target.

When exploring long-horizon latent trajectories, coarse-to-fine steering—capturing global trends via temporal pooling before adding residual corrections—effectively avoids the curse of dimensionality.
Approximating robot geometry using collision spheres and normalizing reward components using offline dataset statistics provides a robust foundation for multi-objective reward engineering.
limitations: Latent steering is constrained by the representation capacity of the pretrained flow model's trajectory manifold; it cannot discover entirely novel motions that lie far outside the pretraining distribution.

While sim-to-real transfer succeeds zero-shot, performance remains dependent on LiDAR point-cloud reconstruction accuracy and low-level MPC tracking fidelity; experiments did not evaluate scenarios with rapidly moving dynamic obstacles.
